title: TSMC CEO Sees No Ceiling on Profitability After Record AI-Driven Quarter
excerpt: Record NT$763 billion profit, a raised 44% full-year growth outlook and $52.3-$54.3 billion fourth-quarter guidance signalled no slowdown in AI chip demand.
body:
• TSMC reported record third-quarter net income of about NT$763 billion, up roughly 69% year over year on revenue of NT$1.49 trillion ($46.72 billion).
  • Chief executive C.C. Wei said leading-edge demand was extremely robust, saw no sign of a slowdown, and raised full-year 2026 revenue growth guidance to about 44% in dollar terms.
  • Fourth-quarter revenue is guided at $52.3-$54.3 billion, with gross margin forecast at 65-67%.
  • Reader utility: advanced technologies (7nm and below) made up 79% of wafer revenue — the AI demand signal investors in Nvidia, Apple and Indian IT supply chains track most closely.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's largest contract chipmaker, reported a record third quarter on Thursday and told analysts it sees no sign of a slowdown in demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure — and no ceiling on its long-term profitability, though it cautioned that major margin gains will not arrive overnight.

Chairman and chief executive C.C. Wei described leading-edge demand as extremely robust on the earnings call and raised the full-year outlook, according to MarketWatch coverage of the results. The company now expects revenue growth of about 44 percent in dollar terms for 2026, up from a previous view of slightly over 40 percent.

"And we did not see any sign of slowdown."

— C.C. Wei, Chairman and CEO, TSMC

Record numbers

Invezz reported net income of NT$763.06 billion for the September quarter, up 68.7 percent from a year earlier and above the NT$746.3 billion LSEG SmartEstimate. Revenue rose 50.9 percent to NT$1.49 trillion, and diluted earnings were NT$29.43 a share, or $4.60 per ADR. The Financial Economy's results analysis put revenue at $46.72 billion, above the top of TSMC's own guidance range.

Profitability held up despite concerns about the cost of ramping newer technology and overseas factories. Gross margin was 66.4 percent, operating margin 58.7 percent and net margin 51.1 percent. Advanced technologies accounted for 79 percent of wafer revenue, with 3-nanometre chips contributing 33 percent, 5nm 28 percent and the newer 2nm process 8 percent.

Guidance points higher

Chief financial officer Wendell Huang guided fourth-quarter revenue to between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, a 58 percent year-over-year increase at the midpoint and above the roughly $51.18 billion analysts had expected. Gross margin is forecast at 65 to 67 percent for the quarter.

TSMC kept its 2026 capital expenditure budget at $60 billion to $64 billion and said spending from 2026 to 2028 would be significantly higher than in the previous three years. The company is investing $265 billion in Arizona factories, including an additional $100 billion announced in July, with volume production expected to start in the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of schedule. Management acknowledged that overseas factories currently dilute gross margin by about two percentage points, a drag that could widen as Arizona and Japan scale up.

Agentic AI as the next demand leg

Wei pointed to rising adoption of agentic AI — systems that act as assistants rather than simple chatbots — as a fresh source of demand, including for central processing units tied to those workloads. That matters because it broadens the AI build-out beyond the accelerators that have driven the current cycle.

The results arrived after a sharp sell-off in technology shares, driven by hotter U.S. inflation data and doubts about whether hyperscalers can earn back their AI spending. TSMC's New York-listed shares fell 1.5 percent in premarket trading and its Taiwan shares closed 2 percent lower, showing that a record quarter alone did not settle the valuation debate.

What it means

TSMC is the clearest single gauge of physical AI demand: if its order book were weakening, the slowdown would show here first. On Thursday's evidence it is not — guidance rose, advanced nodes dominate sales, and management is still spending heavily on capacity. The open questions are cost and returns, not demand: tool price inflation, overseas-fab dilution and whether customers' AI investment produces enough revenue to sustain orders into 2027 and beyond.

For technology investors, the next checks are TSMC's monthly sales in early November, which will show whether the fourth-quarter ramp is on track, and customer commentary from Nvidia and Apple on accelerator demand.
